stops.name: Broad Street, the death of Robert
stops.campa: Robert sickens of consumption and William nurses him without sleep for the last fortnight, sitting at the bedside until his own body gives out with exhaustion and grief. At the moment of death William sees, plain before him, his brother's released spirit rise up through the plain matter-of-fact ceiling of the room, clapping its hands for joy at the moment of its release. It is not sorrow alone he carries out of that room but a fact: that the body's ending is not the spirit's, seen with his own eyes, in his own house, over his own brother.
stops.quote_source: Blake's own account of Robert's death, recorded in Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 6

stops.name: Poland Street, Robert's spirit teaches the secret of illuminated printing
stops.campa: A year after the death, Robert comes again, not clapping now but teaching: in a vision, William's dead brother shows him the whole method he has been groping toward, a way of writing his poems and drawing his designs together directly on copper in a liquid that resists the acid, so that when the plate is etched the words and images stand up in relief, ready to print, while all else bites away. Blake rises the next morning, buys the materials the vision named, and it works exactly as shown. Illuminated printing, and with it the illuminated books, are given him this way, complete.

stops.name: Poland Street, Songs of Innocence printed
stops.campa: With the method Robert gave him, Blake etches, prints, and with Catherine hand-colors the first copies of Songs of Innocence: the Piper on the hill who lays down his pipe at a child's request and writes his happy songs in a book that all may read, the Lamb, the Chimney Sweeper's dream of an Angel with a bright key. Each copy is a unique object, no two colored quite alike. He is at once author, engraver, printer and illuminator of his own book, a whole trade folded into one man and one household, exactly as the vision on Broad Street promised.
stops.quote: Piping down the valleys wild, / Piping songs of pleasant glee, / On a cloud I saw a child, / And he laughing said to me: / 'Pipe a song about a Lamb!'

stops.name: Hercules Buildings, Lambeth, the workshop of prophecy
stops.campa: The Blakes move south of the river to a larger house in Hercules Buildings, Lambeth, with room enough for a press and a garden Blake is said to sit naked in with Catherine, reading Paradise Lost aloud to a startled visitor, unashamed as Adam and Eve. Here for a decade he will print nearly all his great illuminated books. The French Revolution has just broken out across the water; Blake wears the bonnet rouge in the London streets in sympathy, and begins, on these presses, to build in verse and copper a whole answering mythology of England's own fall and promised redemption.

stops.name: Lambeth, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
stops.campa: At the Lambeth press Blake etches The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, and a Devil, called to account in the Memorable Fancies, answers the Angel not with apology but with scripture of his own, printed in the infernal method, by corrosives, which in Hell are salutary and medicinal, melting apparent surfaces away and displaying the infinite which was hid. The Voice of the Devil declares Energy the only life, and Reason its outward bound; the Proverbs of Hell are read out plate by plate as the Devil's own gospel, and Blake gives it to the reader as fact, not fable.
stops.quote: The road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom. ... Energy is Eternal Delight.
stops.quote_source: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, 'The Voice of the Devil' and 'Proverbs of Hell' (c. 1790-1793)

stops.name: Lambeth, Visions of the Daughters of Albion and America a Prophecy
stops.campa: Two prophetic books come off the Lambeth press in the same season. In Visions of the Daughters of Albion, Oothoon, ravished and chained by Bromion, cries out against every law that binds desire, and Blake gives her cry the standing of scripture. In America a Prophecy, the fiery rebel Orc, chained beneath the Atlantic, rises against the tyrant Albion's Angel and the war for the colonies is refought as the first eruption of the energy that Urizen's cold laws had bound down. The mythology of a fallen and warring Albion, invented whole in this house, is now fully launched.
stops.quote: The soul of sweet delight can never be defiled.
stops.quote_source: Visions of the Daughters of Albion, plate 8 (1793)

stops.name: Lambeth, Songs of Experience and the Book of Urizen
stops.campa: Blake binds Songs of Experience to Songs of Innocence as the two contrary states of the human soul, the Tyger burning against the Lamb, the Sick Rose against the blossoming one. In the same year The First Book of Urizen gives the mythology its dark demiurge entire: Urizen, the cold self-shut architect of law and measurement, exiled from the other Eternals, sets his compasses over the void and begins to build the fallen world of rule and limit. Blake etches him full length in the frontispiece, an ancient bearded lawgiver dividing the darkness with an instrument, the enemy the whole prophetic corpus will now answer.
stops.quote: Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night, / What immortal hand or eye / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

stops.name: Lambeth, Europe a Prophecy and the fall of Albion
stops.campa: Europe a Prophecy carries the mythology across the Channel: Enitharmon, Albion's fallen female portion, casts her false sleep of eighteen centuries over the earth while Los, the eternal prophet and smith, labors at his furnaces against her, and Orc's fire finally breaks out as the French Revolution across the water. The frontispiece shows the Ancient of Days himself leaning from a burning disc of sun, dividing the deep with golden compasses, an image Blake will color and recolor to his last years, the fallen creator caught in the very act of drawing the limit he cannot see beyond.

stops.name: Lambeth, Vala, or The Four Zoas begun
stops.campa: Blake begins the vast unillustrated manuscript he first calls Vala and later The Four Zoas, an attempt to gather the whole scattered mythology, Urizen, Luvah, Tharmas, Urthona and his emanations, into a single epic of the fall and eventual resurrection of the primeval man Albion, of whom England and every reader is a fallen member. He writes it on the backs of proof sheets for Edward Young's Night Thoughts, revising for years without ever engraving it whole or letting it go to press. It is the deepest working of the private scripture, and it will never, in his lifetime, leave the manuscript state.

stops.name: Felpham, the cottage by the sea
stops.campa: At the invitation of the poet William Hayley, who promises a year's steady work and the run of his library, Blake and Catherine move down from London to a thatched cottage at Felpham on the Sussex coast, the only long exile of his life from the city that made him. He writes to Flaxman within days that heaven opens here on all sides her golden gates, that voices of celestial inhabitants are heard more distinctly and their forms seen more clearly than ever in London's smoke, and that his old friends the Villagers of Felpham, ordinary rustic figures, appear to him now as gods of the mountains and the sea.
stops.quote: Felpham is a sweet place for study, because it is more spiritual than London. Heaven opens here on all sides her golden gates... voices of Celestial inhabitants are more distinctly heard, & their forms more distinctly seen.

stops.name: Felpham, Milton's shade enters Blake's foot
stops.campa: Walking in the garden at Felpham, Blake sees the dead poet John Milton descend as a falling star out of the zenith, swift as a swallow, and enter him bodily through the left foot at the tarsus, a visitation he will set down whole in the epic he calls simply Milton. The elder poet has come, the poem says, to correct the errors of his own theology and to redeem his sixfold emanation, and the living poet's body becomes, for the length of the vision, the very ground the dead one walks to be healed. Blake writes for years afterward inside that entered foot.
stops.quote: Then first I saw him in the Zenith as a falling star, / Descending perpendicular, swift as the swallow or swift; / And on my left foot falling on the tarsus, entered there.
stops.quote_source: Milton, a Poem, plate 15 (composed and etched 1804-1810, the vision set at Felpham)

stops.name: Felpham, the letter of the fourfold vision
stops.campa: Writing to his patron Thomas Butts back in London, Blake sets down in verse, plain as a letter home, the whole ladder of his seeing: single vision, the flat sleep of Newton and Locke that most men never wake from; twofold vision, always granted him; threefold, the soft vision of Beulah's night; and fourfold, his own supreme delight, in which the world stands open all the way to Eternity at once. He asks God to keep him from ever falling back to single sight, as if it were a soul's true danger, worse than any illness Felpham's damp air can give him.
stops.quote: Now I a fourfold vision see, / And a fourfold vision is given to me; / Tis fourfold in my supreme delight / And three fold in soft Beulahs night / And twofold Always. May God us keep / From Single vision & Newtons sleep!
